en: The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology maintains a six-kilometer Permanent Danger Zone around Mayon Volcano to protect people from sudden lava flows.
When PAGASA raises Signal Number 3, winds of 89 to 117 kilometers per hour are expected, requiring families to secure loose roofs.
Swimming in the Pasig River is prohibited because high levels of industrial waste and bacteria make the water unsafe for human health.
Living near the West Valley Fault means families must prepare earthquake survival kits, as a magnitude seven tremor could occur without warning.
Stagnant water in discarded tires around your neighborhood breeds Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which transmit the deadly dengue virus during the rainy season.
Hikers climbing Mount Pulag must bring thick jackets because temperatures can drop below freezing at the summit, risking severe hypothermia.
The Philippines sits near the equator, meaning ultraviolet radiation is extremely high at noon and requires sunscreen to prevent skin cancer.
During typhoons, floodwaters can contaminate deep wells with cholera bacteria, so families must always boil drinking water for at least one minute.
Heavy rains in the steep mountains of Benguet province can trigger deadly landslides, so residents must evacuate when continuous rain exceeds three days.
Swimmers in the coastal waters of Palawan should watch for box jellyfish, whose venomous tentacles can cause fatal heart attacks in humans.
Breathing fine ash particles from Taal Volcano can damage children's lungs, so wearing N95 masks is necessary during ashfall events.
Metro Manila's concrete buildings trap heat, creating an urban heat island effect that raises the heat index and increases the risk of heatstroke.
